name: Wangdue Phodrang
tagline: A rebuilt 17th-century dzong on the ridge above two rivers
meta_description: Wangdue Phodrang, Bhutan: the dzong rebuilt after the 2012 fire, Rinchengang village, Bajothang lunch stops, the tshechu, permits and 2026 costs.
summary: Wangdue Phodrang is a district town at about 1,300 m, 30–40 minutes south of Punakha, where a dzong founded in 1638 stands on a ridge above the Punatsang Chhu. The dzong burned in 2012 and was rebuilt and reconsecrated in 2022. Most travellers stop for 1–2 hours on the way to Phobjikha or Trongsa.
intro: Wangdue Phodrang, usually shortened to Wangdue or Wangdi, is the gateway from the Punakha valley to central Bhutan. The dzong sits on a narrow ridge at the point where the Dang Chhu joins the Punatsang Chhu, at about 1,300 m, so it is warm in winter and hot and humid in summer. From here one road runs north to Punakha, and the main highway climbs east towards Phobjikha, Pele La, Trongsa and Bumthang. Almost every central Bhutan itinerary passes through, and many travellers never realise how old the place is.

Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal founded the dzong in 1638, choosing the ridge because it commanded the routes to the south and centre of the country. It stood for nearly 375 years until a fire on 24 June 2012 destroyed most of it. The government and people of Bhutan rebuilt it over the following decade using traditional methods, timber and rammed earth, and it was reconsecrated in 2022. Visiting it now means seeing an old design in new wood, with the paint still bright.

The old bazaar below the dzong has largely moved to a planned new town at Bajothang, a few kilometres down the river, which is where you will find most shops, petrol and lunch places. The valley floor has also been busy for years with the Punatsangchhu hydropower works, so expect dust and lorries on some stretches. Stay in Punakha or Lobesa and visit Wangdue as a stop. Wangdue needs a route permit, like Punakha, and a licensed guide; check current status before you travel.

story.title: Wangdi's palace and the four ravens
paras: Two traditions explain why the dzong stands where it does. The first is about the name. Bhutanese tradition says that when Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal came to this ridge, he met a boy named Wangdi playing in the sand by the river, and named the place Wangdi's palace, Wangdue Phodrang, after him. The second is about the site. As the Zhabdrung was looking for the right place to build, four ravens are said to have flown up from the ridge in the four directions, which was taken as a sign that religion would spread from here across the country.

The history is firmer. The dzong was founded in 1638, a year after Punakha Dzong was completed, as part of the Zhabdrung's chain of fortresses that held the newly unified state together. Wangdue controlled the routes to the south and to central Bhutan, and its governor, the Wangdue Dzongpon, was one of the important officials of the old system. The building was enlarged over the centuries and long housed both the district administration and a monk body.

On 24 June 2012 a fire broke out and spread through the dry timber, destroying most of the dzong. Many of its religious treasures were carried out in time. Rather than leave a ruin, Bhutan rebuilt it on the same plan, with carpenters, masons and painters trained in the traditional way, and it was reconsecrated in 2022. Your guide may point out the difference between the new structure and old stones that survived.
story.source: Wangdue Phodrang Dzong and Wangdue Phodrang articles (Wikipedia); Department of Culture, Ministry of Home Affairs, Bhutan; Kuensel reporting on the 2012 fire and the reconstruction

did_you_know: Wangdue Phodrang Dzong was founded by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal in 1638.
A fire on 24 June 2012 destroyed most of Wangdue Phodrang Dzong; it was rebuilt using traditional methods and reconsecrated in 2022.
Phobjikha valley, home to the wintering black-necked cranes, lies inside Wangdue Phodrang district.
facts: The rebuilt dzong, Rinchengang village, the tshechu, gateway to central Bhutan

highlights.title: The rebuilt dzong
highlights.text: Founded in 1638, burned in 2012 and reconsecrated in 2022, Wangdue Phodrang Dzong now stands on its ridge in new timber and fresh paint on the old plan. Walk the courtyards with your guide and ask about the rebuilding; it is a rare chance to see traditional construction this new.

highlights.title: Rinchengang village
highlights.text: A compact village of rammed-earth houses on the hillside facing the dzong, reached by a short walk up from the road. Local tradition links it to the builders of the dzong. It is one of the best-preserved clustered villages in western Bhutan.

highlights.title: Lunch in Bajothang
highlights.text: The planned new town of Bajothang, a few kilometres downriver, is the practical stop for lunch, cash and petrol on the way to Phobjikha or Trongsa. Simple restaurants serve set meals of red rice, ema datshi and dal at local prices.

highlights.title: The Wangdue Tshechu
highlights.text: The autumn tshechu, held by the lunar calendar around September or October, is known for the Raksha Mangcham, the dance of the ox, and ends with the unfurling of a large thangka. It is smaller and less crowded than the Thimphu festival.

highlights.title: Gateway to the centre
highlights.text: From Wangdue the highway climbs east towards Nobding, the turn for Phobjikha and Pele La. If you are heading for the cranes or for Bumthang, this is where the central Bhutan part of your trip begins.

how_to_reach.text: Wangdue is about 20 km and 30–40 minutes south of Punakha's Khuruthang, and about 70 km and 2.5 hours from Thimphu over Dochula. Phobjikha is about 60 km and 2–2.5 hours further east via Lawa La. A Bhutan-registered car with driver costs about ₹4,500–6,500 a day, indicative 2026; check current status before you travel.

Wangdue is covered by the same route permit as Punakha, issued by the immigration office in Thimphu on working days and arranged by your operator. A licensed guide is required beyond the first checkpoint for both Indian and international visitors. Check current status before you travel.

The nearest airport is Paro, about 4.5 hours by road. Overland from India, take a train to NJP or Hasimara, cross at Jaigaon–Phuentsholing, and reach Thimphu the same day; Wangdue is then an easy stop on the drive to Punakha or Phobjikha.

where_to_stay: We rarely suggest sleeping in Wangdue itself, because Punakha and Lobesa, 20–30 minutes away, have a wider choice of certified hotels and better settings by the river and the rice terraces. In the Punakha valley, Hotel Lobesa is a reliable budget-to-mid option and Dhensa Boutique Resort a comfortable one, and Amankora and COMO have premium lodges in the area. There are a few certified hotels around Wangdue and Bajothang, mostly plain 3-star properties used by business travellers and groups heading east. If you are going on to Phobjikha the same day, eat lunch in Bajothang and keep driving.
costs: Free; guide's time included in your daily rate
budget_tip: Visit Wangdue as a stop on the Punakha–Phobjikha drive rather than giving it its own day; you see the dzong and Rinchengang in two hours without paying for an extra night of hotel and SDF.
tips: Wangdue at 1,300 m is hot from May to September, so visit the dzong in the morning and carry water.
Fill up on cash in Bajothang or Punakha before heading to Phobjikha, where ATMs are limited.
Dress for the dzong in long sleeves and long trousers or a skirt, and keep cameras down inside temples.
Expect dust and lorries on the valley road near the hydropower works, and keep car windows closed on those stretches.
If you visit during the tshechu, ask your operator where it is held that year and arrive early for a seat.

experiences.title: Wangdue Phodrang Dzong after the rebuild
experiences.summary: A guided walk through the dzong founded by the Zhabdrung in 1638, destroyed by fire in 2012 and rebuilt in the traditional way. You see fresh woodwork and painting on a 17th-century plan, and hear how Bhutan rebuilt it.
body: The dzong stands on a long, narrow ridge where the Dang Chhu meets the Punatsang Chhu, with steep drops on both sides. It was founded by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal in 1638 and became one of the main fortresses of his new state, controlling the way south and the road into central Bhutan. For nearly four centuries it housed the district administration and a monk body, and it was one of the best-known dzongs in the country for its setting.

On 24 June 2012 a fire destroyed most of the building. Bhutan chose to rebuild it on the same plan, and the work took about ten years, with traditional carpenters, masons and painters using timber, stone and rammed earth. The dzong was reconsecrated in 2022. Walking through it now, the woodwork is pale and the paintings bright, and your guide can explain which parts are new and which old foundations survived.

Allow under an hour. Visit in the morning, before the valley heats up, and combine it with lunch in Bajothang and the walk to Rinchengang. Usual dzong rules apply: long sleeves, long trousers or skirt, no caps, and no photographs inside the temples. Opening hours depend on official and religious work, so let your guide confirm the day's timings.

faqs.q: Is Wangdue Phodrang Dzong open after the fire
faqs.a: Yes. The dzong was destroyed by fire in June 2012, rebuilt over about ten years in the traditional way and reconsecrated in 2022. It again houses offices and monks, and visitors can enter with a licensed guide during opening hours. Fees and timings change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How old is Wangdue Phodrang Dzong
faqs.a: The dzong was founded by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal in 1638, a year after Punakha Dzong was completed. The building you see today is largely a reconstruction finished in 2022, on the original plan and with some surviving foundations, after the fire of 24 June 2012 destroyed most of the old structure.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Wangdue Phodrang Dzong
faqs.a: Around 45 minutes to an hour is enough for the courtyards and the main temple with a guide. Most travellers visit it on the way between Punakha and Phobjikha, adding lunch in Bajothang and, if time allows, the short walk to Rinchengang village, for a stop of about two hours in all.

experiences.title: Walk up to Rinchengang village
experiences.summary: A short climb to a clustered village of rammed-earth houses on the hillside facing Wangdue Phodrang Dzong. It is one of the oldest and best-kept villages in the area, with a fine view of the dzong ridge.
body: Rinchengang sits on the slope across the river from the dzong, a tight cluster of two- and three-storey houses with thick rammed-earth walls, wooden windows and shingle or metal roofs. Most Bhutanese villages are spread out across their fields; Rinchengang is unusual because its houses stand close together, with narrow lanes between them. Local tradition says the village was home to the builders and stonemasons who worked on the dzong.

From the road, a footpath climbs through fields and orchards to the village in 20–30 minutes. It is a steady uphill walk but not difficult. Walk quietly through the lanes with your guide, who can ask if a family is happy for you to look inside a house or at the altar room. You will see chillies drying on roofs in autumn, and people weaving or working in the fields.

From the top of the village, look back across the valley to the dzong on its ridge, one of the best views of the rebuilt building. The walk is free and takes about an hour and a half including the climb and time in the village. Go in the morning or late afternoon; midday is hot at this altitude in most months.

faqs.q: How do you get to Rinchengang village
faqs.a: Rinchengang is on the hillside facing Wangdue Phodrang Dzong. Your driver drops you on the road below, and a footpath climbs through fields to the village in about 20–30 minutes. Allow about 1–1.5 hours for the round trip with time in the village. Wear shoes with grip, as the path is dusty and steep in places.

faqs.q: Why is Rinchengang village special
faqs.a: It is a clustered village, with rammed-earth houses packed close together along narrow lanes, unlike most Bhutanese villages where houses are scattered across the fields. It is one of the older villages in the area, and local tradition links it to the builders of Wangdue Phodrang Dzong. It also has a good view of the dzong.

faqs.q: Can I visit a home in Rinchengang
faqs.a: Sometimes, if your guide asks and a family agrees. Do not walk into houses or photograph people without asking. If you are invited in, take off your shoes, accept the butter tea or ara offered, and leave a small gift or a few hundred rupees for the family's altar if it feels right. Many travellers simply walk the lanes.

experiences.title: A local lunch in Bajothang
experiences.best_time: Midday, on the drive to Phobjikha or Trongsa
experiences.image_query: Bhutanese red rice ema datshi lunch
experiences.summary: The practical lunch stop on the road east of Punakha: simple restaurants in Wangdue's new town serving red rice, ema datshi and dal at local prices, plus cash machines, petrol and a chance to buy snacks for the drive.
body: Bajothang is the planned new town of Wangdue Phodrang, a few kilometres down the river from the dzong. Most of the shops and offices that once stood in the old bazaar below the dzong moved here, so it has banks, a few ATMs, petrol, grocery shops and a row of small restaurants. It is not pretty, but it is where drivers and guides eat, which is always a good sign.

A standard lunch is a set meal: red rice, ema datshi (chillies in cheese), kewa datshi (potatoes in cheese), a dal, a green vegetable and sometimes pork, beef or chicken. Ask for the chillies on the side if you do not eat hot food. A meal costs about ₹250–450 per person, indicative 2026, much less than a tourist hotel buffet. Momos and thukpa are also easy to find.

Use the stop to stock up for the road. If you are heading to Phobjikha, buy fruit and biscuits here, take out cash, and use a proper toilet, because the drive up through the forest and over Lawa La has few facilities. Pay in ngultrum or Indian rupees; both are accepted at par, though ₹2,000 notes are not.

faqs.q: Where should I eat between Punakha and Phobjikha
faqs.a: Bajothang, Wangdue's new town, is the best lunch stop. It has several small restaurants serving set meals of red rice, ema datshi, kewa datshi and dal for about ₹250–450 per person, indicative 2026. After Bajothang the road climbs through forest to Phobjikha with only a few roadside stalls, so eat and use the toilets here.

faqs.q: Can I pay in Indian rupees in Wangdue
faqs.a: Yes. The ngultrum is pegged at par to the Indian rupee, and rupees are widely accepted in Bhutan, including in Wangdue and Bajothang. Carry ₹500 and smaller notes. Card payments and UPI are increasingly accepted in towns but are not reliable everywhere, so keep some cash. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Bhutanese food very spicy
faqs.a: Often, yes. Chillies are treated as a vegetable, and ema datshi is chillies cooked in cheese. Restaurants used to tourists will make milder versions or serve chillies on the side if you ask. Kewa datshi, made with potatoes and cheese, red rice, dal and vegetables are usually mild. Tell your guide in advance and they will order for you.

experiences.title: The Wangdue Tshechu and the ox dance
experiences.best_time: Around Sep–Oct, by the lunar calendar
experiences.cost: Free entry; route permit and guide as usual
experiences.summary: Wangdue's autumn religious festival, held over three days around September or October, known for the Raksha Mangcham, the dance of the ox, and the unfurling of a large thangka at dawn on the last day. It is smaller and calmer than the Thimphu Tshechu.
body: Like most dzongs in Bhutan, Wangdue holds an annual tshechu, a festival of masked dances performed by monks and laymen in honour of Guru Rinpoche. Wangdue's is held over three days in the 8th lunar month, which usually falls in September or October, close to the dates of the Thimphu Tshechu. Villagers from across the district come in their best gho and kira, with picnic lunches, to watch the dances and receive blessings.

The festival is known for the Raksha Mangcham, the dance of the ox, and on the final morning a large thangka, a thongdrel, is unfurled before sunrise. Seeing it is believed to bring merit. Because it overlaps with the Thimphu festival, it draws fewer tourists, and you can often get a better view and a more local atmosphere.

During the rebuilding of the dzong, the festival was held at a ground outside the old town, so ask your operator where it is being held in your year. Dates are set by the lunar calendar and change every year. Dress modestly, do not walk across the dance ground, and keep flash off. Hotels in Punakha fill early for these dates, so book ahead.

faqs.q: When is the Wangdue Phodrang Tshechu
faqs.a: It is held over three days in the 8th month of the Bhutanese lunar calendar, which usually falls in September or October, around the same time as the Thimphu Tshechu. Exact dates change every year. Ask your operator for the current calendar before booking, and reserve Punakha hotels early for those dates. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is special about the Wangdue Tshechu
faqs.a: It is known for the Raksha Mangcham, the dance of the ox, and for the large thangka unfurled at dawn on the last day. It is smaller and more local than the Thimphu Tshechu, so you are more likely to sit among village families than tour groups. Entry is free; you need your usual route permit and guide.

faqs.q: Can I combine the Thimphu and Wangdue festivals
faqs.a: Often yes, because they fall in the same lunar month and the two towns are about 2.5 hours apart over Dochula. A common plan is a day at the Thimphu festival, then a drive to Punakha and a morning at Wangdue's. Dates vary each year, so ask your operator to check both calendars before you fix the trip.

faqs.q: Is Wangdue Phodrang worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, as a stop of 1–2 hours. The rebuilt dzong, founded in 1638 and reconsecrated in 2022 after the 2012 fire, is worth seeing, and the short walk to Rinchengang village gives you one of the best views of it. You pass through Wangdue on the way to Phobjikha or Trongsa anyway, so it costs you very little time.

faqs.q: How far is Wangdue from Punakha
faqs.a: About 20 km, or 30–40 minutes by car, from Punakha's Khuruthang town along the Punatsang Chhu. Lobesa, where many Punakha hotels are, is slightly closer. Most travellers visit Wangdue in the morning on the way to Phobjikha, or as a half-day trip from a Punakha hotel.

faqs.q: What happened to Wangdue Phodrang Dzong
faqs.a: A fire on 24 June 2012 destroyed most of the dzong, which had stood since 1638. Many religious objects were saved. Bhutan rebuilt it on the original plan using traditional methods and materials over about ten years, and it was reconsecrated in 2022. It is again in use by the district administration and monks.

faqs.q: Do I need a separate permit for Wangdue
faqs.a: Wangdue is covered by the same route permit as Punakha and Phobjikha, which your operator gets from the immigration office in Thimphu on a working day. If you are going further east to Trongsa or Bumthang, that is added to the permit. A licensed guide is required. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Should I stay in Wangdue or Punakha
faqs.a: Stay in Punakha or Lobesa. The Punakha valley has more certified hotels across budgets, a nicer setting by the rivers and rice terraces, and the main sights within a short drive. Wangdue is 20–30 minutes away and easy to see as a stop. Sleep in Wangdue only if a group booking or festival dates make it necessary.

faqs.q: How far is Phobjikha from Wangdue
faqs.a: About 60 km and 2–2.5 hours by car. The road climbs east from Wangdue through forest towards Nobding, then turns off over Lawa La and drops into the Phobjikha valley at about 2,900–3,000 m. In winter the upper road can be icy early in the morning. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Wangdue Phodrang
faqs.a: At about 1,300 m Wangdue is one of the warmer places on the usual route. Winters are mild, around 15–20 °C by day, while May to September is hot and humid with monsoon rain from June. October to April is the most comfortable time. It is several degrees warmer than Thimphu and much warmer than Phobjikha.

faqs.q: What does Wangdue Phodrang mean
faqs.a: Phodrang means palace. Bhutanese tradition says that Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal met a boy called Wangdi playing by the river when he came to the site, and named the place after him, so the name is usually given as Wangdi's palace. Another tradition tells of four ravens flying out from the ridge in four directions.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM in Wangdue
faqs.a: Yes. Bajothang, Wangdue's new town, has bank branches and ATMs, and is a sensible place to take out cash before Phobjikha or Trongsa, where machines are fewer and can be offline. Foreign cards do not always work in Bhutanese ATMs, so carry some cash in US dollars or rupees as a backup.
